questions.body: In Java, what happens when an object reference is passed as an argument to a method and reassigned inside that method?
questions.keyPoints: Java is strictly pass-by-value; reference values are copied.

options.text: The caller's reference remains unchanged because Java is strictly pass-by-value; a copy of the reference address is passed.
options.explanation: Java is strictly pass-by-value. When an object is passed, a copy of the reference address is passed. Reassigning the copy inside the callee method does not affect the caller's variable.

options.text: The caller's reference points to the new object because references in Java are passed by reference.
options.explanation: Java does not have pass-by-reference. Only the reference value (pointer address) is passed by value.

options.text: A compile-time error occurs unless the method parameter is explicitly declared final.
options.explanation: Method parameters do not have to be final to be reassigned inside method scope.

options.text: Both the caller and callee reference point to null after the method invocation completes.
options.explanation: The caller reference remains untouched pointing to its original object.

questions.keyPoints: intern() returns the string constant pool canonical reference.

options.text: s1 == s3 && s1.equals(s2) && s1 != s2
options.explanation: s1 points to the pool instance. s2 creates an explicit new heap object (s1 != s2). s2.intern() returns the canonical instance from the pool (s1 == s3). Content comparison via equals() is true.
s1 == s2 is false because s2 was created using new String() on the heap.

options.text: s1 != s3 && s1.equals(s2)
options.explanation: s1 != s3 is false because s2.intern() returns the existing pool object s1.
s2 == s3 is false because s2 is on the regular heap while s3 points to the pool.

questions.keyPoints: IntegerCache caches boxed values between -128 and 127 inclusive.

options.text: true false
options.explanation: Autoboxing utilizes Integer.valueOf(), which caches values in the range [-128, 127]. Thus a and b refer to the exact same cached object (true). Values above 127 allocate distinct objects on the heap (false).

options.text: true true
options.explanation: Values above 127 are not cached by default and create separate object references.

options.text: false false
options.explanation: Values within [-128, 127] are guaranteed to be cached, so a == b evaluates to true.

options.text: false true
options.explanation: Caching applies to lower numbers, not higher numbers.

questions.body: What adverse behavior occurs if an entity class overrides `equals(Object o)` to compare business fields, but fails to override `hashCode()`?
questions.keyPoints: Equal objects must have equal hash codes; failure breaks hash-based collections.

options.text: Equal instances may produce distinct hash codes, preventing HashMap or HashSet from locating previously stored keys.
options.explanation: The hashCode contract requires that if a.equals(b), then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). Without an override, default identity hash code places equal instances into different buckets, causing contains() and get() to return null/false.

options.text: The Java compiler emits a compilation error requiring both methods to be overridden simultaneously.
options.explanation: The compiler does not enforce the contract; it is a logical and behavioral runtime contract.

options.text: HashMap throws an IllegalStateException upon invoking map.put().
options.explanation: HashMap executes normally without throwing an exception, leading to silent bugs.

options.text: The equals() method will always return false when invoked by collections.
options.explanation: equals() itself functions as written, but it will never be called if the hash code lands in an empty or different bucket.

questions.body: When is a `static` initialization block (`static { ... }`) executed in a Java class?
questions.keyPoints: Static initializers run once per class loading and initialization.

options.text: Exactly once when the class is loaded and initialized by the JVM class loader.
options.explanation: Static blocks execute when the class is initialized by the class loader, prior to any instances being created or static methods/fields being accessed.

options.text: Every time a new instance of the class is instantiated with the new keyword.
options.explanation: Instance initialization blocks run on every constructor call, not static initialization blocks.

options.text: Immediately before every static method invocation on that class.
options.explanation: Static blocks run only once upon class initialization, not before every method call.

options.text: When the class is loaded into memory by the garbage collector.
options.explanation: Garbage collection manages memory deallocation, not class loading initialization.

questions.body: What guarantee is provided when a reference variable is declared as `final` in Java?
questions.keyPoints: final prevents reference reassignment; it does not make the object mutable fields immutable.

options.text: The reference variable cannot be reassigned to point to another object after initialization.
options.explanation: A final reference variable cannot be rebound to another instance. However, if the underlying object is mutable (e.g. ArrayList), its internal state can still be modified.

options.text: The referenced object becomes deeply immutable and its internal fields cannot be changed.
options.explanation: final on a variable only restricts reference reassignment, not object state mutation.

options.text: The object is allocated in the thread stack instead of the heap.
options.explanation: Objects are allocated on the heap regardless of whether the reference variable is final.

options.text: The variable can be accessed by multiple threads without any memory visibility issues.
options.explanation: While final fields in constructed objects have safe publication guarantees, declaring a local or shared reference final does not replace general thread synchronization.

questions.keyPoints: Binary arithmetic promotions promote operands smaller than int to int.

options.text: Compilation failure: cannot convert from int to byte without an explicit cast.
options.explanation: In Java binary arithmetic (+), operands smaller than int (byte, short, char) are promoted to int. Therefore, (b + 1) produces an int, which cannot be assigned to byte without explicit cast (byte)(b + 1) or compound operator (b++ / b += 1).

options.text: Compiles successfully and b becomes 11.
options.explanation: Automatic narrowing from int to byte is not performed for arithmetic expressions without explicit cast.

options.text: Throws an ArithmeticException at runtime.
options.explanation: This is a compile-time type mismatch error, not a runtime arithmetic exception.

options.text: b wraps around to -128 due to byte boundary overflow.
options.explanation: Overflow only occurs when the value exceeds byte range after valid assignment.

questions.body: Which of the following exceptions is an unchecked exception in Java that does not require mandatory catch or throws declaration?
questions.keyPoints: Subclasses of RuntimeException are unchecked.

options.text: IllegalArgumentException
options.explanation: IllegalArgumentException directly inherits from RuntimeException, categorizing it as an unchecked exception. It signals improper argument usage without mandatory throws declarations.

options.text: IOException
options.explanation: IOException directly extends java.lang.Exception and is a checked exception requiring explicit handling.

options.text: SQLException
options.explanation: SQLException extends java.lang.Exception and is a checked exception.

options.text: ClassNotFoundException
options.explanation: ClassNotFoundException extends java.lang.Exception and is a checked exception.

questions.body: In the standard HotSpot JVM runtime data area, where are local primitive variables and method activation records stored?
questions.keyPoints: Method frames and local primitive variables reside on the thread's JVM stack.

options.text: In the thread-private JVM Stack frame.
options.explanation: Each Java thread possesses its own JVM Stack. When a method is called, a frame is pushed onto the stack containing local variables (primitives and object reference pointers) and operand stacks.

options.text: In the shared Heap memory space.
options.explanation: The Heap stores actual object instances and arrays shared across all threads.

options.text: In Metaspace alongside class metadata.
options.explanation: Metaspace stores class definitions, method bytecode, and static constant pools.

options.text: In the Program Counter register.
options.explanation: The PC register merely maintains the address of the currently executing JVM instruction.

questions.body: Which of the following is considered an active Garbage Collection (GC) Root in Java?
questions.keyPoints: Active thread local variables, JNI references, and system classes serve as GC roots.

options.text: Local variables and parameter references currently active in a thread's call stack frame.
options.explanation: Objects referenced by active stack frames in any executing thread are GC Roots. If an object is reachable via a chain of references starting from a GC Root, it cannot be collected.

options.text: Any two objects referencing each other in a circular chain with no external references.
options.explanation: Circular references without a path from a real GC Root are isolated islands and are collected by tracing GC.

options.text: WeakReference objects whose referent has not been marked as phantom.
options.explanation: Weak references do not prevent referents from being reclaimed during garbage collection.

options.text: Transient fields of a non-serialized object residing in the old generation.
options.explanation: Field modifiers like transient affect serialization, not GC root status.

questions.body: What does the expression `Integer a = 127; Integer b = 127; System.out.println(a == b);` print versus `Integer c = 128; Integer d = 128; System.out.println(c == d);`?
questions.keyPoints: IntegerCache caches values between -128 and 127.

options.text: `true` followed by `false`
options.explanation: Java's `IntegerCache` pre-caches Integer objects in the range `[-128, 127]`. For 127, both reference the cached instance (== is true). For 128, new distinct objects are allocated (== is false).

options.text: `true` followed by `true`
options.explanation: 128 falls outside the default byte-range IntegerCache.

options.text: `false` followed by `false`
options.explanation: Values up to 127 are cached.

options.text: `false` followed by `true`
options.explanation: The cached range is below 128.

questions.body: What is the size and default value of a `char` primitive in Java?
questions.keyPoints: 16-bit unsigned Unicode character; default value is '\u0000'.

options.text: 16-bit (2 bytes) unsigned integer, with default value `'\u0000'` (0).
options.explanation: Java `char` is a 16-bit unsigned Unicode character (range 0 to 65,535). Its default value is the null character `'\u0000'`.

options.text: 8-bit (1 byte) ASCII character, with default value `' '` (space).
options.explanation: Java uses 16-bit Unicode characters, not 8-bit ASCII.

options.text: 32-bit (4 bytes) UTF-32 code point, with default value `null`.
options.explanation: Primitives cannot be null and char is 16 bits.

options.text: 8-bit signed integer, with default value `0`.
options.explanation: `byte` is 8-bit signed; `char` is 16-bit unsigned.

questions.body: What is the difference between the `>>` and `>>>` operators in Java?
questions.keyPoints: >> is signed shift (preserves sign bit); >>> is unsigned shift (fills top bits with zeros).

options.text: `>>` is an arithmetic signed right shift (preserves the sign bit); `>>>` is a logical unsigned right shift (fills leftmost vacated bits with 0s regardless of sign).
options.explanation: For negative numbers, `>>` propagates 1s to preserve negativity. `>>>` shifts zeros into the high-order bits, converting negative numbers into large positive numbers.

options.text: `>>>` shifts by 3 bits at a time; `>>` shifts by 2 bits.
options.explanation: Both shift by the number of bit positions specified by the right operand.

options.text: `>>>` can only be applied to floating point numbers.
options.explanation: Bitwise shift operators cannot be applied to floats or doubles.

options.text: `>>` is deprecated in Java 17.
options.explanation: Both shift operators are standard Java language features.

questions.body: Which statement accurately describes the distinct uses of `final`, `finally`, and `finalize` in Java?
questions.keyPoints: final is a keyword modifier; finally is a try-catch block; finalize is a deprecated Object method.

options.text: `final` is a keyword to restrict modification (constants, non-overridable methods, un-extendable classes); `finally` is a block in exception handling; `finalize` is a deprecated method in `Object` for cleanup.
options.explanation: `final` applies to variables/methods/classes. `finally` executes after try/catch. `finalize()` is deprecated for removal since Java 9/18 in favor of `Cleaner` and `AutoCloseable`.

options.text: `final` and `finally` are exact synonyms.
options.explanation: One is a declaration modifier; the other is control-flow syntax.

options.text: `finalize` is called every time a variable goes out of scope.
options.explanation: `finalize()` was invoked nondeterministically by the GC before reclamation.

options.text: `finally` blocks are skipped if an unhandled exception occurs.
options.explanation: `finally` blocks execute even when exceptions are thrown.

questions.body: What happens when an `int` value `130` is explicitly cast to a `byte` in Java (`byte b = (byte) 130;`)?
questions.keyPoints: Narrowing primitive conversion truncates to lowest 8 bits: 130 becomes -126 in two's complement.

options.text: `b` becomes `-126` due to two's complement overflow of the 8-bit signed byte range `[-128, 127]`.
options.explanation: `130` in binary is `...0000 1000 0010`. Truncating to 8 bits gives `1000 0010`. The leading 1 denotes negative; two's complement calculation gives `-128 + 2 = -126`.

options.text: A runtime `ArithmeticException` is thrown.
options.explanation: Java primitive casts wrap silently without throwing exceptions.

options.text: `b` is clamped to the maximum byte value of `127`.
options.explanation: Java does not perform saturating arithmetic; it truncates bits.

options.text: `b` becomes `130`.
options.explanation: A signed byte cannot hold values above 127.

questions.body: In modern Java switch expressions (`switch (...) -> ...`), what keyword is used to return a value from a multi-line block branch?
questions.keyPoints: yield is used to produce a value from a switch block.

options.text: `yield`
options.explanation: Java 14 introduced switch expressions. Inside a multi-line `{ ... }` block of a switch case, the `yield` statement specifies the evaluated return value of the switch expression.

options.text: `return`
options.explanation: `return` exits the enclosing method, not just the switch expression.

options.text: `break`
options.explanation: `break` was used in preview versions, but finalized Java syntax uses `yield`.

options.text: `output`
options.explanation: `output` is not a Java keyword.

questions.body: What does declaring a `record Person(String name, int age) {}` automatically provide in Java 16+?
questions.keyPoints: Immutable data carrier class with private final fields, constructor, getters (name(), age()), equals, hashCode, and toString.

options.text: An immutable class with private final fields, canonical constructor, accessor methods (`name()`, `age()`), and auto-generated `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()` implementations.
options.explanation: Java records are transparent, immutable data carriers that eliminate boilerplate for value classes. All fields are private final and records cannot extend other classes (they implicitly extend `java.lang.Record`).

options.text: A mutable JavaBean with `getName()` and `setName()` methods.
options.explanation: Record fields are immutable and accessors omit the 'get' prefix (e.g. `person.name()`).

options.text: A database table entity mapped directly to JPA.
options.explanation: Records are pure language-level data constructs, not JPA entities.

options.text: A class that can be extended by other classes.
options.explanation: Records are implicitly `final` and cannot be extended.

questions.body: What delimiter is used to declare multi-line Text Blocks in Java 15+?
questions.keyPoints: Triple double-quotes: """ followed by a line terminator.

options.text: Triple double quotes: `"""`
options.explanation: Text blocks are enclosed in `"""` and must be followed by a newline on the opening line, preserving internal formatting and stripping common incidental whitespace.

options.text: Backticks: ```
options.explanation: Backticks are used in JavaScript and Go, not Java.

options.text: Triple single quotes: `'''`
options.explanation: Single quotes in Java are exclusively for `char` literals.

options.text: `<<TEXT ... TEXT` heredoc syntax.
options.explanation: Heredoc syntax is used in Bash/PHP/Perl, not Java.

questions.body: What are the rules regarding the placement and number of Varargs parameters (`Type... args`) in a Java method signature?
questions.keyPoints: Only one varargs parameter is permitted, and it MUST be the last parameter.

options.text: A method can have at most ONE varargs parameter, and it MUST be the last parameter in the method signature.
options.explanation: Java enforces `void foo(int a, String... names)`. If varargs were permitted in earlier positions or multiple times, argument binding would be ambiguous.

options.text: A method can have multiple varargs parameters as long as they have different types.
options.explanation: Only one varargs parameter is permitted per method.

options.text: The varargs parameter must be the FIRST parameter in the signature.
options.explanation: It must strictly be the last parameter.

options.text: Varargs parameters can only accept primitive types.
options.explanation: Varargs work with both primitives and object references.

questions.body: How does Pattern Matching for `instanceof` (Java 16+) simplify conditional type casts?
questions.keyPoints: Binds a typed pattern variable directly in the condition: if (obj instanceof String s).

options.text: It binds a typed pattern variable directly in the `if` condition: `if (obj instanceof String s) { s.length(); }`, eliminating redundant explicit casting.
options.explanation: Pattern matching for `instanceof` tests the type and scopes a pattern variable `s` whose scope flows into true branches, avoiding boilerplate like `String s = (String) obj;`.

options.text: It converts runtime casts to compile-time macros.
options.explanation: It tests types at runtime and automatically introduces the typed variable.

options.text: It allows matching against regular expressions.
options.explanation: It matches object types, not text regexes.

options.text: It replaces `try...catch` blocks.
options.explanation: It is an enhancement to the `instanceof` operator.
